_note: Content for BEYOND THE ARCHIVE. All facts come from the sources listed with each block (read 14-15 Nov 2026). Our own educational explanations are marked kind: 'interpretation'. The activities are educational only: nothing done on this website is sent to NASA, MoonDiff or Zooniverse. No verified Lunar Orbiter / LRO image pair could be obtained, so the Moon comparison is a clearly labelled ILLUSTRATION, not imagery. See docs/research-sources.md.

hero.title: Beyond every mission lies another discovery.
hero.tagline: The next discovery could begin with you.
hero.subtitle: Two worlds. Different scientific questions. Countless opportunities to explore.
hero.narrative: We have explored the footprints humanity left behind on the Moon and Mars. But exploration does not end when a mission ends. Scientists continue to investigate these worlds, and people around the world can participate in some of that scientific work.
hero.objective: Investigate how scientific observations help us understand the Moon and Mars, and discover how you can participate in real planetary research.

principles.title: Uncertainty
principles.text: What can I not confidently conclude? Saying so is a valid scientific answer.

moon.name: Moon
moon.opening: Decades separate these observations. What changed on the Moon while humanity was looking away?

points: Five NASA Lunar Orbiter missions photographed 99% of the Moon in 1966–1967.
The cameras exposed film, developed it on board, then scanned it and radioed it to Earth, where it was recorded on analog magnetic tape.
Selected areas were photographed at high resolution, down to about 2 m per pixel.
From 2008, the Lunar Orbiter Image Recovery Project worked with NASA to digitise the images from the degrading tapes.

eras.label: 2009–today
points: LRO arrived in 2009 and has delivered imagery continuously; MoonDiff's team wrote in February 2023 that it was still flying.
Its digital cameras see detail as fine as about half a metre.
By comparing LRO images with other LRO images, the LRO team found 222 impact craters that appeared during LRO's first 14 years.

moon.whyHumans: LRO images can be compared with each other automatically, because they share similar geometry and lighting. Comparing 1960s Lunar Orbiter film with modern LRO images is different: the pictures were taken from different angles, in different lighting, and do not line up well. MoonDiff's team says that kind of change detection is "beyond the capabilities of today's cleverest software", so it uses "the human brain's vision system".
questions: What's the meteorite impact cratering rate?
Where are the missing spacecraft crash sites?
What kind of geologic changes are happening right now on the lunar surface?

compare.title: How a comparison works
compare.illustrationLabel: Illustration, not real lunar imagery. Drawn shapes show the techniques MoonDiff volunteers use. They are not observations.

steps.title: 1 · Align
steps.text: Before volunteers see a pair, MoonDiff's team map-projects and coregisters it. Without that step, a feature in the LRO image can appear several kilometres away in the Lunar Orbiter image. Drag the slider to line up the two illustrated frames.

steps.title: 2 · Blink or fade
steps.text: Volunteers compare pairs side by side, or by blinking or fading between them, so that anything that changed seems to jump out. Blink the aligned frames, or fade between them.

steps.title: 3 · Flag a change
steps.text: In MoonDiff, volunteers draw a polygon around an area that changed. Here, click the spot you think changed.

compare.found: You spotted the crater that appears only in the newer frame. In MoonDiff, this would be flagged as a possible change, not yet a discovery.
compare.falseAlarm: That mark is in the old frame only, but it is a film scratch, not a change on the Moon. The real Lunar Orbiter images were scanned from film and reassembled from strips by hand, so they contain distortions and artefacts. Look for a crater that appears only in the newer frame.
compare.missed: Nothing changed there. Blink again and look for a crater that appears only in the newer frame.
compare.limitation: Why an illustration? We could not obtain a verified, published, co-registered pair of Lunar Orbiter and LRO images, and building one ourselves from raw archive data would not be authentic. Real pairs are available only inside MoonDiff.

lookFor.title: New impact craters
lookFor.text: Space rocks hit the Moon and blast new craters. MoonDiff aims to measure how often that happens.

lookFor.title: Other surface changes
lookFor.text: Rocks break off and roll down hills; MoonDiff's team also asks what geologic changes are happening right now.

lookFor.title: Spacecraft hardware
lookFor.text: Spaceships land and spaceships crash. NASA says volunteers might spot historical objects, like the missing ascent stage of the Apollo 11 lunar lander.

lookFor.title: Things that only look like changes
lookFor.text: Different sun angles, viewing angles and old-film artefacts can make an unchanged area look different. That is why lunar experts review every identified change.

lab.credit: NASA/Goddard/Arizona State University, "LRO Finds Apollo 16 Booster Rocket Impact Site"
lab.instrument: Taken by the high-resolution Narrow Angle Camera (LROC) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
lab.researching: After decades of uncertainty, NASA identified the crater left when Apollo 16's S-IVB rocket stage was deliberately crashed into the Moon. Seismometers left by earlier Apollo crews measured these impacts to study the Moon's interior.
lab.alt: Grey lunar surface seen from orbit, with many small craters and one crater surrounded by bright rays near the centre.

questions.q: Look at the centre of the image. Which statement is an observation?
options: There is a crater surrounded by bright rays
A rocket stage made this crater
Not enough evidence to decide
questions.best: There is a crater surrounded by bright rays

feedback.There is a crater surrounded by bright r: Yes. That is what the image directly shows: an observation.
feedback.A rocket stage made this crater: That is an interpretation. The image alone shows a rayed crater; it cannot show what made it.
feedback.Not enough evidence to decide: Fair. Try describing only what you can see: shape, brightness, pattern. That is an observation.

questions.q: What might have made the rayed crater?
options: Something hit the surface here: a space rock or a spacecraft
It was painted onto the image
Not enough evidence to decide
questions.best: Something hit the surface here: a space rock or a spacecraft

feedback.Something hit the surface here: a space: A reasonable interpretation. On the Moon, space rocks blast new craters, and spacecraft land and sometimes crash. The image alone cannot say which.
feedback.It was painted onto the image: There is no evidence for that. It is a real orbital photograph from LRO's Narrow Angle Camera.
feedback.Not enough evidence to decide: Also reasonable. We know craters form when something hits the surface, but not from this image alone what hit it.

questions.q: From this image alone, could a natural space rock have made this crater?
options: Yes, the image alone cannot rule it out
No, it is obviously human-made
Not enough evidence to decide
questions.best: Yes, the image alone cannot rule it out

feedback.Yes, the image alone cannot rule it out: Right. NASA linked this crater to Apollo 16 using more evidence than one picture: the Apollo-era tracking estimate pointed to the area, and the crater was finally found about 30 km from that estimate.
feedback.No, it is obviously human-made: That is an assumption. Natural impacts also make rayed craters. NASA needed the Apollo-era tracking estimate plus LRO imagery, and the site was about 30 km from the estimate.
feedback.Not enough evidence to decide: A good scientific answer. The image alone cannot tell you; NASA used extra evidence, including the Apollo-era tracking estimate.

questions.q: A MoonDiff volunteer sees a bright spot in the new image that is not in the 1967 image. Is it a confirmed new crater?
options: Yes, it is a discovery
Not yet: it is a possible change that experts will review
Not enough evidence to decide
questions.best: Not yet: it is a possible change that experts will review

feedback.Yes, it is a discovery: Not yet. In MoonDiff, lunar experts review each identified change in a separate review tool before anything is written up as a discovery.
feedback.Not yet: it is a possible change that ex: Exactly. Volunteers flag possible changes; lunar experts review each one, and discoveries are written up as scientific papers.
feedback.Not enough evidence to decide: That is the honest starting point. In MoonDiff, a flagged spot is a candidate until lunar experts review it.

canCannot.can: This image can show a crater's shape, size and bright rays.
canCannot.cannot: It cannot, on its own, show what made the crater, or when.

lab.projectLink: In MoonDiff you apply the same thinking: flag what you observe, and let lunar experts review what it means.

connect.intro: Lunar imagery and the history of the hardware in our archive are connected: the same orbital cameras that search for new craters have photographed the places where explorers left equipment. But MoonDiff has not confirmed the location or condition of any object in our archive.

items.text: Eagle's bottom half is still at Tranquility Base. Its top half, the ascent stage, carried the crew back to orbit, and NASA calls it "missing". It is one of the historical objects MoonDiff volunteers might spot.
This mirror is still used by scientists on Earth. Orbital imaging is one way to study a site without going near equipment that is still in use.
Surveyor 3 shows why comparing over time matters: Apollo 12 astronauts visited it 31 months after it landed, and its returned parts showed what the lunar environment had done to them.

continue.headline: Ready to explore real lunar imagery?
after: MoonDiff opens on NASA's Moon Trek site, which offers sign-up, a tour and an intro video.
You review real "before and after" pairs: Lunar Orbiter (1967) against LRO.
You compare them side by side, or by blinking or fading, and draw a polygon around anything that changed.
Lunar experts review each identified change. Discoveries will be written up as scientific journal papers, with contributors credited as authors or in the acknowledgements.
continue.mustSubmit: Real classifications can only be made on MoonDiff itself. Nothing on Lunar Echoes is sent to MoonDiff or NASA.
continue.record: I opened the official project: record it in my journal

imageInfo: LRO Finds Apollo 16 Booster Rocket Impact Site
The Apollo 16 S-IVB impact crater, on Mare Insularum about 160 miles (260 km) southwest of Copernicus crater, at 1.921° N, 335.377° E
Not stated in NASA's image record
A crater with bright rays near the centre: the site where Apollo 16's S-IVB rocket stage hit the Moon
LRO had already found the impact sites of the Apollo 13, 14, 15 and 17 boosters; Apollo 16's stayed elusive because radio contact was lost before impact
Seismometers left by earlier Apollo crews measured the energy of these deliberate impacts to study the Moon's interior; knowing where each booster hit completes that record

mars.name: Mars
mars.selectLine: Investigate cloud formations in the Martian atmosphere
mars.opening: Mars may look silent from a distance. But above its surface, an atmosphere is constantly revealing clues.
maven: MAVEN stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. It entered orbit around Mars on 21 September 2014.
It has produced a wealth of data about how Mars' atmosphere responds to the Sun and the solar wind, and how these interactions can explain the loss of the Martian atmosphere to space.
In October 2024, NASA said MAVEN was still taking new data.
whyClouds: Clouds help regulate Mars' climate, just as on Earth: they can reflect incoming sunlight, which cools, and absorb heat the planet gives off, which warms.
Classifying cloud types helps researchers understand the availability of water vapour, wind patterns and Mars' daily weather.
Knowing today's atmosphere is essential for understanding Mars' past climate and how it evolved.
Basic questions are still open: what are the daily, seasonal and yearly patterns in Martian cloud shapes?
mars.credit: NASA/LASP/CU Boulder, image processing by Kyle Connour
mars.instrument: Images of Mars from NASA's MAVEN spacecraft, as used in Cloudspotting on Mars: Shapes.
mars.alt: Two views of Mars from orbit. Left: a globe covered in swirls and streaks of white cloud, with a thin red line near the right edge. Right: a globe where dust and cloud mix into large pale features, with craters visible in the lower half.
mars.caption: Left: Martian clouds in many forms, lit by the Sun from the right; the red line marks the change from day to night. Right: dust and clouds mixing into huge features that cross large parts of Mars. Craters are easy to see in the lower half, where the air is clearer.

shapes.name: Disk cloud
shapes.text: Round, bright clouds. Volunteers check the surface view underneath, because a volcano, a patch of surface ice or a crater can look similar.

shapes.name: Vortex cloud
shapes.text: Clouds that curl in on themselves like a spiral, a little like a hurricane on Earth, though without the same destructive energy.

shapes.name: Streak cloud
shapes.text: Long, narrow, mostly straight clouds of roughly the same width. Sometimes their shadow is visible too.

shapes.name: Gravity-wave clouds
shapes.text: Clouds that form in rows, appearing and disappearing in a preferred direction.

shapes.name: Twilight cloud
shapes.text: Clouds high enough to stay lit by the Sun after the ground beneath them has gone dark, just past the day–night line.

questions.q: In the left view, near the right edge, which statement is an observation?
options: There is a thin red line
The Sun is setting there right now
Not sure
questions.best: There is a thin red line

feedback.There is a thin red line: Yes, that is what you can see. The project explains what it means: the line is drawn to mark where day turns into night. It is a marker, not a cloud.
feedback.The Sun is setting there right now: That is an interpretation. The visible fact is a thin red line; the project explains that it marks the change from day to night.
feedback.Not sure: Fair. Describe only what you can see: a thin red line. What it means comes from the image's documentation.

questions.q: Bright white shapes stand out against the darker disk. What might they be?
options: Possibly clouds: they reflect ultraviolet light strongly
Definitely snow lying on the ground
Not sure
questions.best: Possibly clouds: they reflect ultraviolet light strongly

feedback.Possibly clouds: they reflect ultraviole: A good interpretation. In these ultraviolet images, clouds reflect strongly and appear white, though surface ice can look similar too.
feedback.Definitely snow lying on the ground: Too certain. White can be cloud or surface ice, which is why volunteers check a second view of the surface.
feedback.Not sure: Fair. White suggests cloud in these ultraviolet images, but surface ice can look similar.

questions.q: In the right view, there are large pale features near the top. Are they clouds?
options: Definitely clouds
Possibly clouds, dust, or a mix of both
Not sure
questions.best: Possibly clouds, dust, or a mix of both

feedback.Definitely clouds: That is an assumption. NASA's caption says dust and clouds mix to create these huge features, so pale does not automatically mean cloud.
feedback.Possibly clouds, dust, or a mix of both: Good reasoning. NASA's caption describes dust and clouds mixing here; the image alone cannot separate them.
feedback.Not sure: A valid answer. Even NASA's caption describes these as dust and clouds mixing together.

questions.q: You spot a round white feature. Can you call it a disk cloud straight away?
options: Yes, round and white means disk cloud
Not yet: check whether it is surface ice, a volcano or a crater
Not sure
questions.best: Not yet: check whether it is surface ice, a volcano or a crater

feedback.Yes, round and white means disk cloud: Not yet. The project asks volunteers to check that what they see isn't a volcano or a patch of ice on the surface, using a second view of what lies underneath.
feedback.Not yet: check whether it is surface ice: Exactly. The project's field guide shows round white features that turned out to be surface features, not clouds.
feedback.Not sure: Honest, and the right instinct. In the real project, you check the surface view before you decide.

canCannot.can: These images can show bright features, their shapes, and where they sit relative to day and night.
canCannot.cannot: On their own they cannot always separate cloud from dust, ice or terrain. That takes a second view and careful comparison.

lab.projectLink: In Cloudspotting on Mars: Shapes you apply the same thinking: check the surface view, then tag the cloud shapes you can support.

connect.intro: Every Mars machine in our archive worked on the surface, at one spot, under this sky. MAVEN watches from orbit, across the whole planet. The surface and the atmosphere are two sides of the same story.

items.text: Viking 1 studied Martian weather from the ground: a boom on one of its legs carried temperature, wind-direction and wind-speed sensors.
Phoenix was sent to the Martian arctic partly to study polar climate and weather, and the lower atmosphere above it.
The atmosphere decided Opportunity's fate: it sent its last message as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover.
Dust from the atmosphere slowly covered InSight's solar panels until it could no longer make enough power.

continue.headline: Want to help researchers investigate the Martian atmosphere?
after: The project runs on Zooniverse. NASA says it is open to everyone with an internet-enabled computer, with no sign-up deadline.
Complete the tutorial first (about 10–15 minutes) and read the field guide on Mars' cloud formations.
Then examine MAVEN images and click to tag clouds of each common type.
Your classifications help build a database of when and where these cloud shapes appear.
continue.mustSubmit: Real classifications can only be submitted on Zooniverse. Nothing on Lunar Echoes is sent to Zooniverse or NASA.
continue.note: This is Cloudspotting on Mars: Shapes. NASA also runs a separate, original Cloudspotting on Mars project.
continue.record: I opened the official project: record it in my journal

NASA's MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN)
The project's images come from MAVEN's Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrograph (IUVS), according to its science pages. NASA's caption for this particular image does not name the instrument.
The atmosphere of Mars, seen across the planet's disk
Left: clouds in many forms, lit by the Sun from the right; the red line marks day turning to night. Right: dust and clouds mixing into huge features; craters show where the air is clearer.
Project images are built by scanning across the disk of Mars, so the planet can look cut into strips with some sections repeated
IUVS whole-disk images measure water-ice and dust in the atmosphere; clouds reflect ultraviolet strongly and appear white
